claims.text: In samples/.../Design/OrderNotifications.cs at stage-1, OrderPlacedTightlyCoupled has no constructor parameters and creates its EmailNotifier field with new(); OrderNotifications takes an INotifier in its constructor.
OrderService at stage-1 takes IOrderRepository and INotifier, both interfaces declared in DonHang.Domain; OrderService.cs has no using lines and names neither EF Core nor DonHang.Infrastructure.
AuthController.cs at stage-1 has using DonHang.Infrastructure; and takes DonHangDbContext (concrete, DonHang.Infrastructure) and JwtTokenService (concrete, DonHang.Api) in its constructor.

OrdersController@stage-1 takes OrderService (concrete) and IOrderRepository (interface); its using lines include DonHang.Domain, not DonHang.Infrastructure. ASP.NET Core creates the controller; the DI container supplies its constructor parameters.

Creating your own concrete dependency blocks a fake; a passed-in concrete class is usually a smaller concern; many constructor parameters suggest (by SRP) several jobs; reaching into another project's concrete details tightens coupling.

C# using lines are not a complete list: types in the file's namespace or an enclosing one need no using, and global/implicit usings apply to every file; JwtTokenService (DonHang.Api) needs none in DonHang.Api.Controllers.
claims.source_hint: C# docs: using directive; AuthController uses JwtTokenService (DonHang.Api) with no using

claims.text: What DonHang.Infrastructure offers the business layer is mainly its implementations of DonHang.Domain interfaces (EfOrderRepository, LoggingNotifier); DonHangDbContext is the class it uses to do that work.
